Whalley
WAW-lee
n. (the Lancashire Cistercian abbey of 1296, whose abbot John Paslew was executed in 1537 for the Pilgrimage of Grace)
Old English hwael and leah, the clearing by the round hill; recorded in Domesday as Wallei.

Definition · Webster 1828 · Scriptures · Corruption · Roots · Usage · Related

Biblical Definition

Whalley Abbey in the Ribble valley was not founded on its site but moved to it. The Cistercian community had been planted at Stanlow on the Mersey in 1178, a flood-prone and miserable place, and in 1296 it transferred to Whalley, where an ancient parish church already stood with its Saxon crosses in the yard. Building went on for well over a century. The abbey's end was violent: the last abbot, John Paslew, took part in the Pilgrimage of Grace, the northern rising of 1536 against the suppression of the smaller houses and the religious changes behind it, and he was tried and executed in March 1537. Whalley was dissolved that year. The dictionary records Whalley for the rising and the execution, and declines to make the abbot either a hero or a villain. The rebels asked for the old religion, and their instinct that something was being torn up by the roots was not wrong, “Remove not the ancient landmark, which thy fathers have set.” (Pro 22:28) being a real command. But the paths a man is told to ask for are specified, “Stand ye in the ways, and see, and ask for the old paths, where is the good way, and walk therein” (Jer 6:16), and the old way in Jeremiah is the text, not the custom.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines a pilgrimage as a journey to a holy place; a landmark as a mark of boundaries; a rising as an insurrection; ancient as old or of long standing; and a path as a way beaten by feet.

expand to see more

PILGRIMAGE, n. A journey which a person takes to visit some holy place, as to the sepulchre of Christ at Jerusalem.

LANDMARK, n. Any mark or fixed object by which the limits of a farm, a town, or an estate may be known.

INSURRECTION, n. A rising against civil or political authority; the open and active opposition of a number of persons.

ANCIENT, a. Old; that happened or existed in former times, usually at a great distance of time.

PATH, n. A way beaten or trodden by the feet of man or beast; a track.

Key Scripture

Pro 22:28 — "Remove not the ancient landmark, which thy fathers have set."

Jer 6:16 — "Thus saith the LORD, Stand ye in the ways, and see, and ask for the old paths, where is the good way, and walk therein, and ye shall find rest for your souls. But they said, We will not walk therein."

Zec 4:6 — "Then he answered and spake unto me, saying, This is the word of the LORD unto Zerubbabel, saying, Not by might, nor by power, but by my spirit, saith the LORD of hosts."

Rom 3:28 — "Therefore we conclude that a man is justified by faith without the deeds of the law."

Modern Corruption

Cistercian abbey moved from Stanlow in 1296, dissolved in 1537 after its last abbot joined the Pilgrimage of Grace.

expand to see more

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the difference between an old path and an old habit. The rebels of 1536 were defending something, and Scripture does forbid casual demolition: “Remove not the ancient landmark, which thy fathers have set.” (Pro 22:28). But Jeremiah's famous verse names what is to be asked for, “Stand ye in the ways, and see, and ask for the old paths, where is the good way, and walk therein” (Jer 6:16), and the good way there is a way to walk in, revealed, not merely inherited.

The live temptation is to settle the question by force, which both sides tried. Zechariah had already ruled that out for the rebuilding of a house of God: “Not by might, nor by power, but by my spirit, saith the LORD of hosts” (Zec 4:6). And the doctrine actually at stake in the 1530s was not a boundary stone but a sentence, “a man is justified by faith without the deeds of the law” (Rom 3:28), which is why the rising could not have saved what it wanted to save.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew gebul (H1366), a boundary; Hebrew nethibah (H5410), a path; Hebrew chayil (H2428), might; Greek dikaioo (G1344), to justify.

expand to see more

Hebrew gebul (H1366) — a border, a boundary; “Remove not the ancient landmark, which thy fathers have set.”, Proverbs 22:28.

Hebrew nethibah (H5410) — a pathway, a track; “Stand ye in the ways, and see, and ask for the old paths, where is the good way, and walk therein”, Jeremiah 6:16.

Hebrew chayil (H2428) — strength, an army, might; “Not by might, nor by power, but by my spirit, saith the LORD of hosts”, Zechariah 4:6.

Hebrew ruach (H7307) — spirit, breath, wind; “Not by might, nor by power, but by my spirit, saith the LORD of hosts”, Zechariah 4:6.

Greek dikaioo (G1344) — to justify, to declare righteous; “a man is justified by faith without the deeds of the law”, Romans 3:28.

Usage

"“Remove not the ancient landmark, which thy fathers have set.” (Pro 22:28) — what the rebels of 1536 half-rightly defended."

"“Stand ye in the ways, and see, and ask for the old paths, where is the good way, and walk therein” (Jer 6:16) — the old way is the text, not the custom."

"“Not by might, nor by power, but by my spirit, saith the LORD of hosts” (Zec 4:6) — neither side was entitled to settle it by force."
